The Magic Flute. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's The Magic Flute, composed in 1791, is a two-act Singspiel—a German opera form featuring spoken dialogue—that ranks among his most popular and symbolic works. With a libretto by Emanuel Schikaneder, the opera follows Prince Tamino, who is rescued from a giant serpent by the three ladies of the Queen of the Night. The Queen commissions Tamino to rescue her daughter Pamina, who has been captured by the high priest Sarastro. Accompanied by the comic bird-catcher Papageno, Tamino is gifted a magical flute and magic bells to protect them. Upon arriving at Sarastro's temple, Tamino realizes that Sarastro represents wisdom and light, while the Queen of the Night represents darkness and tyranny. Tamino and Pamina undergo trials of silence, fire, and water to achieve spiritual enlightenment and join Sarastro's order, while the Queen is defeated.

Tamino is a foreign prince who falls in love with Pamina's portrait and undergoes initiation trials to prove himself worthy of her. Pamina is the Queen of the Night's daughter, captured by Sarastro for her own protection, who joins Tamino in his final initiation trials. Papageno is a simple, gluttonous bird-catcher clad in feathers who seeks only food, wine, and a Papagena to love. He fails his trials but is rewarded with a wife. Sarastro is the high priest of Isis and Osiris who governs a temple of wisdom and reason, acting as a benevolent guide to Tamino and Pamina. The Queen of the Night, or Königin der Nacht, is Pamina's mother, a personification of dark vengeance who plots to destroy Sarastro's temple. Monostatos is a Moorish temple slave who repeatedly attempts to force himself on Pamina, and later betrays Sarastro to join the Queen of the Night.

The opera features several celebrated musical numbers. Der Hölle Rache kocht in meinem Herzen, meaning Hell's vengeance boils in my heart, is the Queen of the Night's famous Act II coloratura aria, demanding that Pamina assassinate Sarastro. This aria is notorious for its extremely high range, hitting high F above high C. Der Vogelfänger bin ich ja, or The birdcatcher am I indeed, is Papageno's Act I entrance song, introduced by a simple panpipe motif. Dies Bildnis ist bezaubernd schön, meaning This image is enchantingly beautiful, is Tamino's Act I lyrical aria expressing his immediate love for Pamina upon seeing her portrait. O Isis und Osiris is Sarastro's Act II solemn bass aria, calling upon the Egyptian gods to grant wisdom and strength to the new initiates. Pa-pa-pa is the joyful comic duet in Act II where Papageno and Papagena celebrate their reunion and fantasize about raising a large family.

The Magic Flute is saturated with Freemasonry themes and rituals, as both Mozart and Schikaneder were Masons. The opera opens with an overture featuring three solemn chords, reflecting the Masonic importance of the number three, and the trials of the initiates mirror Masonic rites of passage. The Singspiel format allowed the work to reach a broad, popular audience at Vienna's suburban Theater auf der Wieden, rather than the aristocratic court. Notably, it was Mozart's last completed opera, premiering just over two months before his death.
